Japanese Steel Industry Hit as South China Sea Port Blockade Disrupts Exports

A sudden naval blockade imposed by China at key shipping lanes in the South China Sea has severely disrupted Japan’s steel industry, causing widespread delays in exports and raising concerns over supply chain security. The blockade, which began early Monday, targets vessels carrying steel and steel-related materials, including shipments from major firms such as Mitsui & Co Ltd and smaller regional producers.

According to the Japan Iron and Steel Federation, at least 60,000 tonnes of finished steel products scheduled for overseas delivery remain stranded at ports in Yokohama and Kobe. “This action jeopardizes our commitments to clients in Southeast Asia and beyond,” said Kenichi Nakamura, spokesperson for the federation. “Every day of disruption compounds the risk of lost contracts and reputational damage.”

Mitsui & Co Ltd confirmed that several of its export consignments have been affected. In a statement, the company said it is “working closely with government authorities and shipping partners to find alternative routes, but the situation remains highly fluid.”

Export prices for Japanese hot-rolled coil steel surged 7% in spot trading Tuesday amid fears of protracted delays. Analysts at the Tokyo Metal Exchange warned that if the blockade continues, domestic inventories could rise sharply, forcing mills to cut production. “Steel is a cornerstone of Japan’s industrial output. Prolonged export paralysis will inevitably affect margins and growth projections,” said Yuto Sakamoto, senior analyst at Nihon Securities.

The Japanese government has demanded an immediate end to the blockade, calling the action “unacceptable under international law.” No resolution had been reached at the time of writing, and industry officials warned that ongoing disruptions could inflict lasting damage on Japan’s steel export sector.
